description_full: The Hershey Company, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacture and sale of confectionery products and pantry items in the United States and internationally. It operates through three segments: North America Confectionery, North America Salty Snacks, and International. The company offers chocolate and non-chocolate confectionery products; gum and mint refreshment products, including mints, chewing gums, and bubble gums; protein bars; pantry items, such as baking ingredients, toppings, beverages, and sundae syrups; and snack items comprising spreads, bars, snack bites, mixes, popcorn, and pretzels. It provides its products primarily under the Hershey's, Reese's, Kisses, Jolly Rancher, Almond Joy, Brookside, barkTHINS, Cadbury, Good & Plenty, Heath, Kit Kat, Payday, Rolo, Twizzlers, Sour Strips, Whoppers, York, Ice Breakers, Breath Savers, Bubble Yum, Lily's, SkinnyPop, Pirates Booty, Dot's Homestyle Pretzels, and ONE Bar brands, as well as under the Pelon Pelo Rico, IO-IO, and Sofit brands. The company markets and sells its products to wholesale distributors, chain grocery stores, mass merchandisers, chain drug stores, vending companies, wholesale clubs, convenience stores, dollar stores, concessionaires, and department stores. It exports its products in approximately 65 countries worldwide. The Hershey Company was founded in 1894 and is based in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

financial_summary: The Hershey Company is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $35.8B market cap on $11.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 26% against a 6% cost of capital — a 20-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 45%.

The business throws off $1.8B in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.58× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -10.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.4×.

Shareholder yield of 3.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 12% operating margin runs 5pp above the Consumer Defensive median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.53x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-7.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.30, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $233.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 31% in the 2020 crash, 12% in the 2022 bear market and 27% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 10% below its DCF fair value of $198, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $133 to $306 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: EV/EBITDA 12.9 vs 10.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 69% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 21 covering analysts target $181 on average, 2% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 26% clears the cost of capital of 6.0% by 20pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.29).
It runs a 45% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.58x, but high accruals (-10.1% of assets).
ROE of 19% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.5x net debt to EBITDA ($676.7M of cash against $4.9B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.4x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.9% over 3 years, 7.5% over 5 years and 4.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 78%).
At current returns, reinvesting 67% of profits supports about 17.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 7.7% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 3.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 23, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 23.7% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 91%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (132 sales, net $51.4M sold).
It returns 3.0% a year to shareholders (3.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 11.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 17,550 employees, each generates about $666K of revenue, 1.3x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 5.1% a year.
That works out to $104K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (4x revenue per employee).
